name: Kyoto
tagline: Lantern-lit lanes, moss gardens and the soul of old Japan
description:
For more than a thousand years Kyoto was the seat of emperors, and it still behaves like a capital of taste. Its grid of low wooden townhouses hides moss gardens, tea rooms and family businesses that have made fans, knives or tofu for twenty generations. Spared the worst of wartime bombing, the city and its surroundings hold seventeen UNESCO-listed temples, shrines and castles, most within a short bus or train ride of each other.

The trick is timing. The headline sights, Fushimi Inari, Kiyomizu-dera and the Golden Pavilion, are gloriously photogenic and seriously crowded from mid-morning, so see them at opening time or dusk and spend the middle of the day in quieter corners: a Zen rock garden, a sake brewery in Fushimi, a café beside the Kamo River.

Food here is subtle rather than showy: silky yuba, simmered tofu, pickles from Nishiki Market and multi-course kaiseki built around the season. Stay at least three nights, wear shoes you can slip off easily, and treat yourself to a traditional ryokan for at least one of them.

safety.notes: Crime is very low, but temple steps turn slippery in rain and the packed lanes below Kiyomizu-dera attract the occasional pickpocket. Some private lanes in Gion now fine trespassers, so stay on public streets.

tipping: Tipping is not expected anywhere in Kyoto, including ryokan; a heartfelt thank-you in Japanese goes much further.
gettingAround: City buses reach most temples but crawl in peak season, so combine the Karasuma and Tōzai subway lines, JR and the Keihan and Hankyū railways with walking. Rent a bike for the flat paths along the Kamo River.
tips: Visit Fushimi Inari before 07:30 or after dark; the gates never close and the upper mountain is nearly empty once you pass the Yotsutsuji viewpoint.
The old bus-only day pass is gone, so tap an IC card or buy the subway-and-bus day pass, and use trains wherever possible to dodge traffic.
Use a same-day luggage delivery counter at Kyoto Station rather than hauling suitcases onto crowded city buses, where they are unwelcome.
Many temples stop admitting visitors 30 minutes before closing, often around 16:30, so plan your last temple of the day carefully.
Arashiyama empties after 17:00 when day-trippers leave; stay for dusk along the Katsura River and the lantern-lit Togetsukyō Bridge.
Book kaiseki restaurants and tea ceremonies two to four weeks ahead in spring and autumn, and go for lunch, when the same kitchens charge a fraction of dinner prices.
etiquette: Never chase, touch or photograph maiko and geiko without permission; they are working professionals on their way to appointments.
Respect no-photo signs inside temple halls and gardens, and keep your voice low in Zen precincts.
Take off your shoes before stepping onto tatami or into temple halls, and leave them neatly pointing toward the door.
Avoid eating while walking in Nishiki Market and on temple approaches; most stalls provide a spot to stand and finish your snack.

phrases.pronunciation: koh-reh NAHN-boh (Kansai style; standard is 'ikura desu ka?')

phrases.local: お手洗いはどこですか？ (otearai wa doko desu ka?)
お勘定お願いします (okanjō onegai shimasu)

neighborhoods.name: Gion
neighborhoods.blurb: Kyoto's most famous geisha district, with teahouses behind bamboo blinds along Hanamikōji and the willow-lined Shirakawa canal, best explored at twilight.

neighborhoods.name: Higashiyama
neighborhoods.blurb: Sloping stone lanes of Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka climb toward Kiyomizu-dera past pottery shops, tea houses and pagoda views.

neighborhoods.name: Arashiyama
neighborhoods.blurb: Western foothills of bamboo groves, river boats, a monkey park and Zen gardens; magical early in the morning, frantic by noon.

neighborhoods.name: Pontochō
neighborhoods.blurb: A single lantern-lit alley squeezed between Kiyamachi and the Kamo River, crammed with restaurants whose summer platforms hang over the water.

neighborhoods.name: Nishijin
neighborhoods.blurb: The old weaving quarter northwest of the Imperial Palace, with working textile studios, old bathhouses and townhouse guesthouses far from tour groups.

dishes.name: Yudōfu
dishes.description: Cubes of silky tofu warmed in kelp broth and dipped in citrusy ponzu, a Zen-temple dish perfected around Nanzen-ji and Arashiyama.

dishes.name: Obanzai
dishes.description: Kyoto home cooking: small bowls of simmered vegetables, tofu and fish lined up along the counters of neighborhood restaurants.

dishes.name: Nishin soba
dishes.description: Buckwheat noodles in hot broth topped with a sweet-simmered fillet of dried herring, a Kyoto creation from the late 1800s.

dishes.name: Yuba
dishes.description: The delicate skin lifted from simmering soy milk, eaten fresh with a drop of soy sauce, rolled into dumplings or floated in clear soups.

dishes.name: Uji matcha
dishes.description: Stone-ground green tea from nearby Uji, whisked frothy alongside a seasonal wagashi sweet or turned into parfaits and soft-serve.

events.name: Aoi Matsuri
events.description: On May 15 around 500 people in Heian-period court dress parade with ox-drawn carts from the Imperial Palace to the Shimogamo and Kamigamo shrines.

events.name: Gion Matsuri
events.description: Japan's most famous festival fills July; towering wooden floats roll through downtown on the 17th and 24th, and the evenings before are street parties full of food stalls and yukata.

events.name: Gozan no Okuribi
events.description: On the night of August 16, giant bonfires shaped like kanji characters, a torii and a boat are lit on five mountainsides to guide ancestral spirits home.

events.name: Jidai Matsuri
events.description: On October 22 a costumed procession walks backward through a thousand years of Kyoto history, from Meiji-era soldiers to Heian nobles, ending at Heian Shrine.

attractions.name: Fushimi Inari-taisha
attractions.description: Thousands of vermilion torii gates, each donated by a business hoping for prosperity, tunnel up the slopes of Mount Inari. Most visitors turn back after the first photogenic stretch, but the full loop to the summit takes two to three hours and passes quiet sub-shrines guarded by stone foxes.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive before 07:30, or come after sunset when the lanterns glow and the tour groups have gone.

attractions.name: Kinkaku-ji
attractions.description: The Golden Pavilion's upper two floors are sheathed in gold leaf and mirrored in a still pond, a sight that genuinely lives up to the postcards. The route through the grounds is one-way and brisk, so linger at the first pond viewpoint, and come after a snowfall for the most breathtaking photos.
attractions.bookingTip: Be at the gate at 09:00 sharp; by 10:30 the tour buses turn the pond viewpoint into a scrum.

attractions.name: Kiyomizu-dera
attractions.description: The great wooden stage of this hillside temple juts 13 meters above a forested ravine on a lattice of zelkova pillars assembled without nails. Below, sip from one of the Otowa waterfall's three streams for longevity, love or success, and return for the spring and autumn night illuminations.
attractions.bookingTip: Come at the 06:00 opening for an empty stage, then walk down Sannenzaka before the shops and crowds wake up.

attractions.name: Arashiyama Bamboo Grove
attractions.description: Walking among the towering green stalks of this grove, you hear the wind as a soft wooden clatter overhead. The path is only a few hundred meters long, so pair it with Tenryū-ji's garden next door and the hillside Ōkōchi Sansō villa for a fuller morning.
attractions.bookingTip: Take the first JR train to Saga-Arashiyama and be in the grove by 07:00; by 09:30 it is shoulder to shoulder.

attractions.name: Nishiki Market
attractions.description: Nicknamed 'Kyoto's kitchen', this narrow covered arcade runs five blocks with over a hundred stalls selling pickles, rolled dashi omelettes, soy-milk doughnuts and handmade knives. Many vendors sell tasting skewers, and it is the best place for edible souvenirs like sansho pepper and yuzu salt.
attractions.hours: Most stalls 10:00–17:00; some closed Wed or Sun
attractions.bookingTip: Go around 10:00 as the stalls open, and eat snacks where you buy them, since walking while eating is discouraged here.

attractions.name: Gion
attractions.description: Kyoto's best-preserved entertainment district glows at dusk as paper lanterns flicker on outside the wooden teahouses of Hanamikōji and along the Shirakawa canal. You may spot a maiko hurrying to an appointment; admire her from a distance and stay on the public streets.
attractions.bookingTip: Several private lanes off Hanamikōji are closed to tourists with a ¥10,000 fine, so follow the signs.

attractions.name: Philosopher's Path
attractions.description: A two-kilometer stone footpath shadows a cherry-lined canal between Ginkaku-ji and the Nanzen-ji area, named for a philosophy professor who walked it daily in meditation. Small temples, cafés and craft shops appear along the way, and in early April the water fills with drifting petals.
attractions.bookingTip: Walk it north to south, starting at Ginkaku-ji, so you finish near Nanzen-ji's brick aqueduct and a yudōfu lunch.

attractions.name: Nijō Castle
attractions.description: Built for the first Tokugawa shogun, this moated castle is famous for its 'nightingale floors', which chirp underfoot to betray intruders. Inside the Ninomaru Palace, gilded screen paintings of tigers and pines grow grander as you approach the shogun's audience chamber.
attractions.bookingTip: Rent the audio guide at the gate, since the palace rooms have almost no English signage inside.

attractions.name: Kyoto National Museum
attractions.description: The airy Heisei Chishinkan wing displays Buddhist sculpture, tea-ceremony ceramics and scroll paintings that once belonged to the city's temples, while a red-brick Meiji-era hall anchors the garden outside. Its autumn special exhibition is one of Japan's big cultural events.
attractions.bookingTip: Pair it with Sanjūsangen-dō's hall of 1,001 golden Kannon statues directly across the street.

attractions.name: Ryōan-ji
attractions.description: Fifteen rocks set in raked white gravel form Japan's most famous and most debated Zen garden, arranged so you can never see all fifteen at once from the veranda. Afterward, circle the mirror pond and its mossy woodland, which surprisingly few visitors bother to explore.
attractions.bookingTip: Visit right at opening and combine it with Kinkaku-ji, about 20 minutes' walk along the Kinukake-no-michi road.

hotels.name: Suirin Kamogawa
hotels.description: A low-slung retreat on the east bank of the Kamo River, with 40 rooms facing either the water or a moss courtyard. Each suite has a cypress bath and a private engawa veranda, and the kaiseki restaurant sources from farms in the Kyoto countryside.

hotels.name: Nishijin Itoya Machiya
hotels.description: A restored 1910s weaver's townhouse split into four suites, each with a tatami sitting room, a view of a tiny garden and a deep umbrella-pine tub. A local host drops off a Kyoto breakfast basket every morning.

hotels.name: Hotel Higashiyama Kōgei
hotels.description: Each of the 24 rooms was fitted out by a different Kyoto craftsperson, from Kiyomizu-ware tea sets to indigo-dyed headboards. It sits on a lane below Kiyomizu-dera, so you can reach the temple stage long before the crowds.

hotels.name: Kamo Riverside Backpackers
hotels.description: A cheerful hostel in a former textile office with curtained capsule bunks, a big communal kitchen and a terrace facing the river. Staff hand out cycling maps and host a nightly izakaya meet-up for solo travelers.

hotels.name: Arashiyama Tsukikage Onsen
hotels.description: A riverside onsen ryokan where hot-spring water fills open-air cedar tubs overlooking the Hozu gorge. Multi-course dinners are served in your room, and once the day-trippers leave at dusk you will have Arashiyama's lanes almost to yourself.

hotels.name: Inari Fox Apartments
hotels.description: Minimalist one-bedroom apartments five minutes' walk from the torii gates, with washer-dryers, induction kitchens and bikes for the ride to Fushimi's sake breweries. Handy for early starts on the mountain and quick JR hops to Nara.

restaurants.name: Yukimachi
restaurants.description: A ten-seat kaiseki counter inside a former Gion teahouse, where the chef's fourteen courses are plated on ceramics fired in his own kiln. Dinner opens with a sip of cold Fushimi sake and ends with whisked matcha beside a lantern-lit garden.
restaurants.signatureDish: Seasonal hassun platter and charcoal-grilled sweetfish

restaurants.name: Dashimaki Kōbō Suzume
restaurants.description: A standing counter in Nishiki where cooks flip dashi-soaked egg into fluffy rolled omelettes in square copper pans. Order a thick slice on a skewer or tucked into a soft sandwich, and watch the rhythm through the window.

restaurants.name: Kissa Sosui
restaurants.description: A canal-side café in an old farmhouse near the southern end of the path, roasting its own beans and serving thick, fluffy milk-bread toast for breakfast. Window seats look straight onto the cherry trees.
restaurants.signatureDish: Shokupan toast with sweet red bean and butter

restaurants.name: Takebayashi Yudōfu
restaurants.description: Tofu made each morning with local well water is simmered at your table in a kelp-only broth and served with seven small side dishes in a garden pavilion. The whole set is plant-based, and it makes a gentle, warming lunch after the bamboo grove.
restaurants.signatureDish: Yudōfu set with sesame tofu and fresh yuba

restaurants.name: Obanzai Tomoshibi
restaurants.description: Two sisters cook a rotating spread of around twenty obanzai dishes, from simmered daikon to eggplant with white miso, set out in bowls along the counter. Point at whatever catches your eye and pair it with a local craft sake.

restaurants.name: Sannenzaka Soba Kanade
restaurants.description: An old wooden noodle house on the slope below Kiyomizu-dera, serving hand-cut buckwheat noodles in a kelp-and-bonito broth. The nishin soba, topped with sweet-glazed herring, is the thing to order on a cold day.

restaurants.name: Bistrot Shichijō
restaurants.description: A tiny French bistro run by a Lyon-trained chef who cooks with heirloom Kyoto vegetables from farms in the northern hills. Roast duck with sweet Manganji peppers and a well-priced lunch prix fixe make it a smart stop after the museum.

restaurants.name: Kitsune-ya Shokudō
restaurants.description: A cheap, cheerful diner at the foot of the shrine serving kitsune udon topped with sweet fried tofu, plus inari sushi, both named for the fox messengers of the god Inari. The ideal refuel after the summit hike.

experiences.name: Dawn Torii Trail Hike to Inari's Summit
experiences.description: Meet at 06:00 and climb through the gates with a guide who decodes the fox messengers, the donors' inscriptions and the mountain's hidden shrines. You reach the summit before the first tour bus arrives and finish with tea at a family-run teahouse.
includes: Tea and sweets at a mountain teahouse

experiences.name: Gion Lantern Walk with a Former Maiko
experiences.description: A former maiko leads you through Gion's lanes as the lanterns come on, explaining how teahouses work and how an apprentice's hairstyle and kimono change as she rises through the ranks. The walk ends with a question-and-answer session over tea.
includes: Guided walk with an ex-maiko host

experiences.name: Machiya Tea Ceremony & Wagashi Class
experiences.description: Learn the choreography of a traditional tea ceremony in a century-old townhouse, then shape your own seasonal sweets from bean paste under a confectioner's guidance. Small groups mean everyone whisks their own bowl.

experiences.name: Nishiki to Fushimi Sake & Food Walk
experiences.description: Graze through Nishiki with a local food writer, tasting pickles, rolled omelette and soy-milk doughnuts, then hop a train south to Fushimi's sake district for a guided brewery tasting. You'll learn why the area's soft groundwater makes such gentle, rounded sake.
